# Rate Limiting API: A Comprehensive Design Document

## 1. Introduction and Background

In the ever-evolving landscape of distributed systems, the need for robust rate limiting has become increasingly apparent. As our platform continues to scale and serve a growing number of clients, we must ensure that our shared infrastructure remains resilient, fair, and performant. This document presents a thoughtful and thorough design for a new centralized Rate Limiting API that will serve as the backbone of traffic management across our engineering organization.

Rate limiting, at its core, is the practice of controlling the rate at which requests are processed by a system. It serves multiple purposes: protecting backend services from being overwhelmed, ensuring fair resource allocation among tenants, and providing a mechanism for graceful degradation under load. The importance of rate limiting cannot be overstated in modern microservice architectures, where a single misbehaving client can cascade failures across an entire service mesh.

Our current approach to rate limiting is fragmented. Various teams have implemented their own solutions, ranging from simple in-memory counters to Redis-based distributed counters. This fragmentation has led to inconsistent behavior, duplicated effort, and operational blind spots. The Rate Limiting API described herein aims to unify these disparate approaches into a single, well-designed service that all teams can rely upon.

## 2. Historical Context

To fully appreciate the design decisions in this document, it is helpful to understand the journey that has brought us to this point. In the early days of our platform, rate limiting was handled entirely at the load balancer level using simple connection-based limits. As our architecture evolved toward microservices in 2021, individual teams began implementing their own rate limiting logic.

The Payments team was among the first to build a dedicated rate limiter, using a token bucket algorithm backed by Redis. The Search team followed with a sliding window implementation, also Redis-backed but using a different data model. The Notifications team opted for a leaky bucket approach using an in-memory solution with periodic synchronization. Each of these implementations was well-suited to its specific use case, but the proliferation of approaches created significant operational overhead.

In Q3 2023, an incident involving the Search team's rate limiter highlighted the risks of this fragmented approach. A misconfigured rate limit allowed a burst of traffic that overwhelmed a downstream database, causing a 47-minute outage affecting multiple services. The post-incident review recommended a centralized rate limiting solution, which is the genesis of this project.

We also considered adopting an off-the-shelf solution such as Envoy's built-in rate limiting service. After careful evaluation, we determined that our requirements around multi-dimensional rate limiting, dynamic configuration, and deep integration with our existing authentication infrastructure warranted a custom solution. That said, we have drawn significant inspiration from Envoy's rate limiting service design, particularly its descriptor-based approach to defining rate limit rules.

## 3. Design Philosophy

The design of the Rate Limiting API is guided by several core principles that we believe will lead to a robust and maintainable system:

First, simplicity of interface. We believe that the API surface should be as minimal as possible while still meeting the needs of our diverse set of consumers. A simple API is easier to understand, easier to integrate with, and easier to maintain over time.

Second, correctness over performance. While performance is certainly important for a rate limiting service, we prioritize correctness of rate limit enforcement. An inaccurate rate limiter can be worse than no rate limiter at all, as it may give teams a false sense of security.

Third, observability as a first-class concern. The Rate Limiting API should provide rich telemetry that enables teams to understand their traffic patterns, debug issues, and make informed decisions about their rate limit configurations.

Fourth, graceful evolution. The system should be designed to evolve over time without requiring breaking changes to existing integrations. We anticipate that our understanding of rate limiting requirements will deepen as more teams adopt the service.

These principles inform every aspect of the design, from the choice of algorithms to the structure of the API itself.

## 4. System Architecture

The Rate Limiting API is designed as a standalone gRPC service that sits alongside the services it protects. It consists of several key components that work together to provide accurate and performant rate limiting.

The core of the system is the Rate Limit Engine, which is responsible for evaluating incoming rate limit check requests against the configured rules. The engine supports multiple rate limiting algorithms, including token bucket, sliding window, and fixed window. The choice of algorithm is configurable on a per-rule basis, allowing teams to select the approach that best fits their use case.

Beneath the Rate Limit Engine sits the Counter Store, which maintains the current state of all active rate limit counters. The Counter Store is backed by a Redis cluster, which provides the combination of low latency and atomic operations that are essential for accurate distributed rate limiting. We use Redis Cluster in a configuration with three primary nodes and three replicas, providing both horizontal scalability and fault tolerance.

The Configuration Service manages the rate limit rules that govern the behavior of the Rate Limit Engine. Rules are defined in YAML format and stored in our existing configuration management system. Changes to rules are propagated to the Rate Limit Engine within approximately 30 seconds, allowing teams to adjust their rate limits without requiring a service deployment.

The Telemetry Pipeline captures detailed metrics about every rate limit decision and exports them to our standard observability stack. This includes per-rule hit counts, rejection rates, and latency distributions.

Finally, the Admin API provides a RESTful interface for managing rate limit configurations, viewing current counter states, and performing administrative operations such as resetting counters or temporarily disabling rules.

## 5. Algorithm Selection

The choice of rate limiting algorithm has significant implications for the behavior of the system. Each algorithm offers different tradeoffs between accuracy, memory usage, and burst tolerance. This section provides a detailed analysis of the three algorithms supported by the Rate Limiting API.

The token bucket algorithm is perhaps the most widely used rate limiting algorithm. It works by maintaining a virtual "bucket" of tokens that is refilled at a constant rate. Each request consumes one token, and requests are rejected when the bucket is empty. The token bucket algorithm naturally allows for short bursts of traffic up to the bucket size, while enforcing an average rate equal to the refill rate. This makes it well-suited for use cases where occasional bursts are acceptable, such as API endpoints that experience periodic spikes in traffic.

The sliding window algorithm provides more precise rate limiting by tracking the exact timestamps of recent requests. It divides time into small sub-windows and maintains a count of requests in each sub-window. The current rate is calculated by summing the counts across all sub-windows that fall within the current window. This approach provides smoother rate limiting than the fixed window algorithm, at the cost of higher memory usage. It is well-suited for use cases where consistent throughput is important, such as rate limiting access to a database with a fixed connection pool.

The fixed window algorithm is the simplest of the three. It divides time into fixed-duration windows and maintains a counter for each window. Requests are rejected when the counter exceeds the configured limit. The fixed window algorithm is the most memory-efficient, as it only requires a single counter per window. However, it is susceptible to the "boundary problem," where a burst of traffic at the boundary between two windows can result in twice the configured rate being allowed in a short period. Despite this limitation, the fixed window algorithm is appropriate for use cases where approximate rate limiting is sufficient and memory efficiency is a priority.

We recommend that most teams start with the token bucket algorithm, as it provides a good balance of accuracy and burst tolerance. Teams with specific requirements around burst behavior or memory usage should consult with the Rate Limiting team to determine the best algorithm for their use case.

## 6. API Design

The Rate Limiting API exposes a gRPC interface for rate limit checks. The primary RPC is CheckRateLimit, which accepts a set of descriptors that identify the rate limit rule to evaluate and returns a decision indicating whether the request should be allowed or rejected.

The protobuf definition for the service is as follows:

```protobuf
syntax = "proto3";

package ratelimit.v1;

service RateLimitService {
  rpc CheckRateLimit(CheckRateLimitRequest) returns (CheckRateLimitResponse);
  rpc GetCurrentUsage(GetCurrentUsageRequest) returns (GetCurrentUsageResponse);
}

message CheckRateLimitRequest {
  string domain = 1;
  repeated Descriptor descriptors = 2;
  uint32 hits_addend = 3;
}

message Descriptor {
  repeated Entry entries = 1;
}

message Entry {
  string key = 1;
  string value = 2;
}

message CheckRateLimitRequest {
  RateLimitResponse overall_code = 1;
  repeated DescriptorStatus statuses = 2;
}

enum RateLimitResponse {
  UNKNOWN = 0;
  OK = 1;
  OVER_LIMIT = 2;
}

message DescriptorStatus {
  RateLimitResponse code = 1;
  RateLimit current_limit = 2;
  uint32 limit_remaining = 3;
  uint32 duration_until_reset = 4;
}

message RateLimit {
  uint32 requests_per_unit = 1;
  RateLimitUnit unit = 2;
}

enum RateLimitUnit {
  UNKNOWN = 0;
  SECOND = 1;
  MINUTE = 2;
  HOUR = 3;
  DAY = 4;
}
```

The domain field in the request identifies the logical grouping of rate limit rules. Typically, each service defines its own domain. The descriptors field contains one or more descriptors, each of which is a list of key-value pairs that identify the specific rate limit rule to evaluate. The hits_addend field allows callers to indicate that a single request should consume multiple tokens, which is useful for endpoints where the cost of processing varies.

## 7. Configuration Model

Rate limit rules are defined in YAML format and organized by domain. Each domain contains a set of descriptors that map to specific rate limit configurations. Here is an example configuration:

```yaml
domain: api-gateway
descriptors:
  - key: user_id
    rate_limit:
      unit: minute
      requests_per_unit: 100
    descriptors:
      - key: endpoint
        value: /v1/search
        rate_limit:
          unit: second
          requests_per_unit: 10
      - key: endpoint
        value: /v1/payments
        rate_limit:
          unit: minute
          requests_per_unit: 30
  - key: api_key
    rate_limit:
      unit: hour
      requests_per_unit: 10000
```

This hierarchical configuration model allows teams to define both broad and specific rate limits. In the example above, each user is limited to 100 requests per minute overall, with additional per-endpoint limits for specific high-value endpoints. API key-based rate limiting is also supported for external consumers.

Configuration changes are validated before being applied to ensure that they are syntactically correct and semantically valid. Invalid configurations are rejected with a descriptive error message, and the previous valid configuration remains in effect.

## 8. Deployment Architecture

The Rate Limiting API is deployed as a Kubernetes StatefulSet with a minimum of three replicas across three availability zones. Each replica maintains a connection to the Redis cluster and can independently serve rate limit check requests.

The service is fronted by a Kubernetes Service of type ClusterIP, and clients connect to it via our standard service mesh (Istio). This provides automatic load balancing, mutual TLS, and circuit breaking without requiring any additional configuration on the client side.

The Redis cluster is deployed on dedicated nodes with local SSD storage to minimize latency. We use Redis Cluster with six nodes (three primaries and three replicas) distributed across three availability zones. The cluster is configured with a replication factor of one, meaning each primary has exactly one replica in a different availability zone.

## 9. Performance Characteristics

The Rate Limiting API is designed to add minimal latency to the request path. Based on our load testing, the service achieves the following performance characteristics:

At the 50th percentile, rate limit checks complete in under 2 milliseconds. At the 99th percentile, checks complete in under 10 milliseconds. At the 99.9th percentile, checks complete in under 25 milliseconds. The service can sustain a throughput of approximately 50,000 checks per second per replica, for a total cluster capacity of 150,000 checks per second with the minimum three-replica deployment.

These numbers were measured under realistic conditions using a mix of single-descriptor and multi-descriptor requests, with a Redis cluster deployed in the same region as the Rate Limiting API replicas.

## 10. Security Considerations

The Rate Limiting API integrates with our existing authentication and authorization infrastructure. All gRPC connections are secured with mutual TLS via the service mesh, ensuring that only authenticated services can make rate limit check requests.

Authorization is enforced at the domain level. Each service is granted access to one or more rate limit domains via our standard RBAC system. Attempts to check rate limits in a domain that the caller is not authorized to access are rejected. This prevents services from interfering with each other's rate limit configurations or consuming each other's rate limit quotas.

The Admin API requires additional authorization beyond what is needed for rate limit checks. Only members of the service's owning team can modify rate limit configurations, and all configuration changes are logged in our audit trail.

We have also considered the security implications of the rate limiting service itself being a target for denial-of-service attacks. To mitigate this risk, the Rate Limiting API applies its own internal rate limits to incoming requests, ensuring that a misbehaving client cannot overwhelm the service.

## 11. Monitoring and Alerting

The Rate Limiting API exports a comprehensive set of metrics that enable teams to monitor the health and behavior of their rate limits. These metrics are exported in Prometheus format and can be visualized using our standard Grafana dashboards.

We provide a pre-built Grafana dashboard that teams can import to get immediate visibility into their rate limit usage. The dashboard includes panels for request volume, rejection rate, latency distribution, and current counter values. Teams are encouraged to customize this dashboard to suit their specific needs.

Alerting is configured using our standard alerting framework. We provide a set of recommended alert rules that teams can adopt, including alerts for high rejection rates, elevated latency, and Redis connectivity issues.

## 12. Migration Strategy

We recognize that migrating from existing rate limiting solutions to the centralized Rate Limiting API is a significant undertaking. To ease this transition, we have developed a phased migration strategy that allows teams to adopt the new service incrementally.

In the first phase, teams deploy the Rate Limiting API client alongside their existing rate limiter in "shadow mode." In this mode, the client makes rate limit check requests to the new service but does not enforce the results. Instead, it logs the decision alongside the decision made by the existing rate limiter, allowing teams to compare the behavior of the two systems.

In the second phase, teams switch to "enforcement mode," where the Rate Limiting API's decisions are enforced and the existing rate limiter is disabled. Teams should monitor their dashboards closely during this phase to ensure that the new service is behaving as expected.

In the third phase, teams remove their existing rate limiting code entirely, completing the migration to the centralized service.

We estimate that most teams can complete the migration within two to three sprints, depending on the complexity of their existing rate limiting logic.

## 13. Future Directions

Looking ahead, we have identified several areas where the Rate Limiting API can be enhanced to provide additional value:

Adaptive rate limiting, where the service automatically adjusts rate limits based on the current health of downstream services, is a particularly exciting area of exploration. This would allow the system to provide more aggressive protection during periods of degradation while allowing higher throughput during normal operation.

We are also exploring the possibility of supporting rate limiting based on request cost rather than simple request count. This would allow teams to assign different costs to different types of requests, providing more nuanced control over resource allocation.

Finally, we plan to develop a self-service portal that allows teams to manage their rate limit configurations through a web interface, reducing the need for manual YAML editing and configuration deployments.

## 14. Conclusion

The Rate Limiting API represents a significant step forward in our platform's ability to manage traffic and protect shared infrastructure. By providing a centralized, well-designed service that all teams can rely upon, we can eliminate the fragmentation and inconsistency that has characterized our approach to rate limiting thus far.

We believe that the design presented in this document strikes the right balance between simplicity and flexibility, and we are confident that it will serve our needs well as the platform continues to grow. We look forward to working with teams across the organization to bring this vision to life.
